### 27. From assignments to a SWIG

Consider the potential-outcome SCM

$$
\begin{aligned}
X(a)&\leftarrow f_X(\epsilon_X),\\
A(a)&\leftarrow f_A(X(a),\epsilon_A),\\
M(a)&\leftarrow f_M(X(a),a,\epsilon_M),\\
Y(a)&\leftarrow f_Y(a,M(a),\epsilon_Y).
\end{aligned}
$$

The noise terms are mutually independent.


Draw its SWIG, including the fixed intervention value $a$.

<div class="response-space"></div>

::: {.answer-block}
**Solution**

Each assignment supplies the incoming arrows for its left-hand variable. The assignment generating $A(a)$ remains, so $X(a)$ points to $A(a)$. The fixed value $a$, rather than $A(a)$, is an input to $M(a)$ and $Y(a)$.

![](images/02f-exercise-assignments-swig.svg){width=700 fig-align="center" fig-alt="X(a) points to A(a) and M(a). Fixed a points to M(a) and Y(a). M(a) points to Y(a). The random A(a) and fixed a are separate nearby circles."}
:::

### 28. A single intervention from a causal graph

Consider the following causal graph:

![](images/02f-exercise-single-causal.svg){width=700 fig-align="center" fig-alt="X points to A and Y; A points to M; Z points to M; and M points to Y."}

a. Construct the SWIG for an intervention on $A$, with intervention value $a$.

b. Apply causal irrelevance. Redraw the SWIG with simplified labels and explain each change.

c. For each statement below, decide whether it is guaranteed by the model. Explain using the local or global Markov property. When independence is not guaranteed, identify an open path.

$$
\begin{aligned}
A&\mathrel{\perp\!\!\!\perp}Y(a),\\
A&\mathrel{\perp\!\!\!\perp}Y(a)\mid X,\\
A&\mathrel{\perp\!\!\!\perp}Y(a)\mid M(a).
\end{aligned}
$$

d. Decide whether each equality follows from the model. Explain which rule or rules justify it. 

$$
E\{Y(a)\mid A=a,X\}=E\{Y(a)\mid X\},
$$

$$
E\{Y(a)\mid A=a,X\}=E\{Y\mid A=a,X\}.
$$

<div class="response-space"></div>

::: {.answer-block}
**Solution**

**a.** Rename every random variable using $(a)$, and split the intervened node. The arrow from $X(a)$ ends at the random part $A(a)$; the arrow to $M(a)$ begins at the fixed value $a$.

![](images/02f-exercise-single-swig.svg){width=700 fig-align="center" fig-alt="X(a) points to A(a) and Y(a); fixed a points to M(a); Z(a) points to M(a); and M(a) points to Y(a)."}

**b.** The fixed value $a$ is not an ancestor of $X(a)$, $Z(a)$, or $A(a)$. Causal irrelevance therefore gives

$$
X(a)=X,\qquad Z(a)=Z,\qquad A(a)=A.
$$

It is an ancestor of $M(a)$ and $Y(a)$, so their labels retain $a$.

![](images/02f-exercise-single-simplified.svg){width=700 fig-align="center" fig-alt="X points to A and Y(a); fixed a points to M(a); Z points to M(a); and M(a) points to Y(a)."}

**c.** Without conditioning, independence is not guaranteed: the path $A\leftarrow X\to Y(a)$ is open. Conditioning on $X$ blocks this path, giving

$$
A\mathrel{\perp\!\!\!\perp}Y(a)\mid X.
$$

This also follows from the local Markov property for $A$ in the topological order $X,Z,M(a),Y(a),A$: its only parent is $X$. The fixed value $a$ is a constant.

Conditioning on $M(a)$ alone does not block $A\leftarrow X\to Y(a)$, so the third independence statement is not guaranteed. The open paths permit dependence but do not require it for every choice of assignment functions.

**d.** Both equalities follow. The first follows from the conditional independence given $X$ in part c: learning $A=a$ supplies no additional information about $Y(a)$ once $X$ is known. The second follows from consistency, which gives $Y(a)=Y$ whenever $A=a$.
:::

### 29. Multiple interventions

Consider the following causal graph:

![](images/02f-exercise-multiple-causal.svg){width=750 fig-align="center" fig-alt="X points to A and Y; A points to M; M points to B and Y; and B points to Y."}

a. Construct the SWIG for interventions on both $A$ and $B$, with intervention values $a$ and $b$.

b. Apply causal irrelevance. Redraw the SWIG with simplified labels and explain each change.

c. For each statement below, decide whether it is guaranteed by the model. Explain using the local or global Markov property. When independence is not guaranteed, identify an open path.

$$
\begin{aligned}
A&\mathrel{\perp\!\!\!\perp}Y(a,b)\mid X,\\
B(a)&\mathrel{\perp\!\!\!\perp}Y(a,b)\mid X,\\
B(a)&\mathrel{\perp\!\!\!\perp}Y(a,b)\mid X,M(a).
\end{aligned}
$$

d. Decide whether each equality follows from the model. Explain which rule or rules justify it. 

$$
E\{Y(a,b)\mid B(a)=b,X,M(a)\}
=E\{Y(a,b)\mid X,M(a)\},
$$

$$
E\{Y(a,b)\mid A=a,B=b,X\}
=E\{Y\mid A=a,B=b,X\}.
$$

<div class="response-space"></div>

::: {.answer-block}
**Solution**

**a.** Rename every random variable using $(a,b)$, and split both intervened nodes. The incoming arrow from $X(a,b)$ ends at $A(a,b)$; the outgoing arrow to $M(a,b)$ begins at $a$. The incoming arrow from $M(a,b)$ ends at $B(a,b)$; the outgoing arrow to $Y(a,b)$ begins at $b$.

![](images/02f-exercise-multiple-swig.svg){width=800 fig-align="center" fig-alt="X(a,b) points to A(a,b) and Y(a,b); fixed a points to M(a,b); M(a,b) points to B(a,b) and Y(a,b); and fixed b points to Y(a,b)."}

**b.** Neither fixed value is an ancestor of $X(a,b)$ or $A(a,b)$, so these become $X$ and $A$. The fixed value $a$ is an ancestor of $M(a,b)$ and $B(a,b)$, but $b$ is not. Their labels become $M(a)$ and $B(a)$. Both fixed values are ancestors of $Y(a,b)$, so its label retains both.

![](images/02f-exercise-multiple-simplified.svg){width=800 fig-align="center" fig-alt="X points to A and Y(a,b); fixed a points to M(a); M(a) points to B(a) and Y(a,b); and fixed b points to Y(a,b)."}

In particular, $B(a)$ is still generated from $M(a)$ and its original noise term. It is not replaced by $b$.

**c.** The first statement is guaranteed. The path $A\leftarrow X\to Y(a,b)$ is blocked by $X$. The second is not guaranteed: $B(a)\leftarrow M(a)\to Y(a,b)$ remains open when we condition only on $X$. The third is guaranteed because conditioning on $M(a)$ blocks that path.

The third statement also follows from the local Markov property for $Y(a,b)$ in the topological order $X,A,M(a),B(a),Y(a,b)$. Its random parents are $X,M(a)$; $a$ and $b$ are constants. The open path in the second statement permits conditional dependence but does not require it for every choice of assignment functions.

**d.** Both equalities follow. The first uses the conditional independence in part c to remove $B(a)=b$ from the conditioning information.

The second uses consistency. When $A=a$, consistency gives $M(a)=M$, and the calculation generating $B(a)$ also agrees with the original calculation, giving $B(a)=B$. When $B=b$ as well, all inputs to the potential-outcome and original outcome assignments agree, so $Y(a,b)=Y$. This replacement does not require an independence statement involving the original $B$.
:::
